keyQuotes: In an era when technical expertise can become obsolete in just a few years, foundational skills are more important than ever.

Researchers estimate that the 'half-life' of technical skills—the time it takes for half of your acquired knowledge to become outdated—has shrunk from about 10 years in the 1980s to just 4 years today, and could soon shrink to less than 2 years.

mainPoints.explanation: The study finds that individuals with higher foundational skill scores get promoted faster, learn new skills more efficiently, and adapt better to industry changes, while specialized technical skills become obsolete at an accelerating pace.
mainPoints.point: Foundational skills (collaboration, mathematical thinking, adaptability) determine long-term career ceilings more than specialized technical skills.

mainPoints.explanation: Since 2007, the proportion of management job descriptions emphasizing collaboration, coaching, and influence has tripled; jobs combining cognitive abilities with social skills command the highest wage premiums.
mainPoints.point: Social skills are the glue for efficient team collaboration, and the related demand continues to grow.

mainPoints.explanation: It is recommended to assess candidates' learning ability, collaboration, and response to uncertainty through targeted questions during hiring; and to invest resources in early-career development to strengthen communication, collaboration, and learning agility.
mainPoints.point: Enterprises should prioritize foundational skills in hiring and development, rather than focusing solely on specialized knowledge.

mainPoints.explanation: Integrate soft skill development into team culture using tools such as peer feedback, mentoring, and team retrospectives, and recognize and reward thoughtful communication and collaborative problem-solving.
mainPoints.point: Managers can reinforce foundational skills through daily behavioral modeling and system design.

oneSentenceSummary: Based on a large-scale study covering 70 million job transitions, this article demonstrates that in an era of shrinking technology half-lives, foundational skills such as collaboration, mathematical thinking, and adaptability are more decisive of long-term career ceilings and organizational adaptability than specialized technical skills.
originalTitle: 未来五年，比技术更值钱的是这些基础能力
summary: Based on large-scale data from over 70 million job transitions across more than 1,000 occupations in the United States between 2005 and 2019, the article categorizes skills into foundational skills (reading comprehension, basic math, teamwork) and specialized advanced skills (such as blockchain). The study finds that individuals with higher foundational skill scores earn higher wages throughout their careers, get promoted faster, learn new skills more quickly, and adapt better to industry changes. As the half-life of technical skills shrinks from 10 years to 4 years and may drop below 2 years, the importance of foundational skills becomes increasingly prominent. Social skills (communication, empathy, conflict resolution) in particular serve as the glue for efficient team collaboration, and the proportion of management job postings emphasizing collaboration, coaching, and influence has tripled since 2007. The article provides three specific recommendations for leaders: prioritize screening candidates with strong foundational skills during hiring; invest in early-career development to strengthen soft skills; and have managers lead by example to model and reward foundational skill behaviors.
title: In the Next Five Years, These Foundational Skills Will Be More Valuable Than Technical Skills
